title: Kibbeh bil sanieh
subtitle: Baked bulgur and lamb cake with pine nut filling
excerpt: Kibbeh bil sanieh is a baked tray dish of two layers of bulgur and lamb shell with a spiced minced lamb and pine nut filling pressed between them. It is sliced in diamond shapes and comes out of the oven with a slightly crisp top and a moist, meaty interior.
sourceNotes: Claudia Roden, A Book of Middle Eastern Food (1968). Baked kibbeh documented as a home dish throughout the Levant, with variations across Lebanon, Syria, and Palestine. Anissa Helou, Lebanese Cuisine (1994). Kibbeh bil sanieh described as the everyday tray version of the hand-formed fried kibbeh.

recipe.freezeNotes: Cool completely, slice into portions, and freeze. Reheat from frozen in a 180-degree oven for 20 minutes.
recipe.makeAheadNotes: The assembled unbaked dish can be covered and refrigerated for up to 24 hours. Bake straight from the fridge, adding five minutes to the time.

content.text: Kibbeh bil sanieh is a Levantine tray bake of two outer layers made from ground bulgur and raw lamb, with a cooked spiced lamb and pine nut filling sandwiched between. It is sliced like a cake and baked until the top is golden and slightly firm. The contrast between the dense outer shell and the yielding filling is what makes it.
Soak {{bulgur-wheat}} in cold water for 20 minutes, then drain and squeeze out excess water firmly in your hands.

In a food processor, blend {{onion}} (for the shell) until very finely chopped. Add 400 g of {{lamb-mince}}, {{allspice}}, {{cinnamon-ground}}, {{black-pepper}}, and {{sea-salt-fine}}. Process until smooth and paste-like.
Add the squeezed bulgur and pulse until fully combined. The mixture should hold its shape when pressed. If it feels sticky, refrigerate for 30 minutes.
Heat {{olive-oil}} in a frying pan over a medium heat. Add the second portion of finely chopped {{onion}} and fry for eight minutes until soft and golden.

Add 300 g of {{lamb-mince}} for the filling and cook, breaking it up, for five minutes until browned. Add the second measures of {{allspice}} and {{cinnamon-ground}}, season well, and stir. Add {{pine-nuts}} and cook for two more minutes. Remove from the heat and cool.
Preheat the oven to 200 degrees. Grease a 30 x 20 cm baking dish with a little oil.
Divide the kibbeh shell mixture into two equal halves. Wet your hands and press the first half evenly into the base of the dish in a layer about 1 cm thick.
Spread the cooled filling evenly over the base layer. Add the second half of the kibbeh mixture on top and press down gently to seal. Smooth the surface with wet hands.

Using a sharp knife, score the top in a diamond pattern. Dot {{unsalted-butter}} over the surface and bake for 35 to 40 minutes until golden on top and cooked through. Leave to rest for ten minutes before cutting along the scored lines.

items.cause: Shell mixture too dry or not pressed down firmly enough
items.fix: Make sure your hands are wet when pressing the shell layers down. A few cracks are normal and do not affect the result.

items.symptom: The filling leaks out from the sides
items.cause: Too much filling or edges not sealed
items.fix: Press the top layer carefully around the edges to seal. Use slightly less filling if the dish is small.

items.cause: Bulgur was not squeezed dry enough or there is too much lamb
items.fix: Squeeze the soaked bulgur very firmly before combining. The ratio of bulgur to lamb should be roughly equal by weight.

items.symptom: The dish falls apart when sliced
items.fix: Leave to rest for at least ten minutes before cutting. The layers settle as it cools.

content.text: Kibbeh in its many forms is considered the national dish of Lebanon and is central to Syrian and Palestinian cooking as well. Kibbeh bil sanieh, the baked tray version, is the most practical for home cooking: it feeds a crowd, can be made ahead, and does not require the hand-shaping skill of the oval fried version. The word kibbeh comes from the Arabic for ball or hollow, referring to the shell shape. The spice blend of allspice and cinnamon is characteristic of the Levant and appears across many dishes. Pine nuts in the filling are traditional but can be replaced with walnuts if needed.
